```{r, load-data}
# Load and prepare data
## EPT
HS_EPT <- read_csv(here("./CSV Files/Adult HS/Adult HS Infinitive EPT.csv")) %>% 
  mutate(Group = "HS",
         Task = "Production") %>% 
  filter(!Item == "FCT-22")

L2L_EPT <- read_csv(here("./CSV Files/Adult L2L/Adult L2L Infinitive EPT.csv")) %>% 
  filter(!Part_ID == "L2L34") %>% 
  mutate(Group = "L2L",
         Task = "Production") %>% 
  filter(!Item == "FCT-22")


## FCT
HS_FCT <- read_csv(here("./CSV Files/Adult HS/Adult HS Infinitive FCT.csv")) %>% 
  mutate(Group = "HS",
         Task = "Preference") %>% 
  filter(!Item == "FCT-22")

L2L_FCT <- read_csv(here("./CSV Files/Adult L2L/Adult L2L Infinitive FCT.csv")) %>% 
  mutate(Group = "L2L",
         Task = "Preference") %>% 
  filter(!Item == "FCT-22")


## Join datasets
EPT <- rbind(HS_EPT, L2L_EPT)
FCT <- rbind(HS_FCT, L2L_FCT)


# Create master
Master <- rbind(EPT, FCT) %>%
  mutate(Short_Prop = case_when(Short_Prop == "Subject" ~ "Subject of ser",
                                Short_Prop == "Object" ~ "Subject of gustar",
                                Short_Prop == "Preposition" ~ "Object of de",
                                TRUE ~ Short_Prop)) %>% 
  rename(Context = Short_Prop) %>% 
  select(c(Part_ID, Item, Comp_Use, Group, DELE, DELE_Std, Task, Context, Davies_Std, Verb)) %>% 
  mutate(Context = factor(Context, levels = c("Subject of ser", "Subject of gustar", "Object of de")),
         Task = factor(Task, levels = c("Production", "Preference")))
```


```{r, generate-graph-dataframes}
# Prepare averages for graphs
## Bar graph
Master_Bar <- Master %>% 
  filter(!is.na(Comp_Use)) %>%
  group_by(Group, Task, Context) %>% 
  summarize(Total_Accuracy  = sum(Comp_Use, na.rm = TRUE),
            Total_Responses = n(),
            Ratio = 100 * Total_Accuracy / Total_Responses,
            .groups = "drop")


## Violin plot
Master_Violin <- Master %>% 
  filter(!is.na(Comp_Use)) %>% 
  group_by(Part_ID, Group, Task, Context) %>% 
  summarize(Total_Accuracy  = sum(Comp_Use, na.rm = TRUE),
            Total_Responses = n(),
            Ratio = 100 * Total_Accuracy / Total_Responses,
            .groups = "drop")

Master_Violin$Context <- factor(Master_Violin$Context, levels = c("Subject of ser", "Subject of gustar", "Object of de"))


## Averages and SD
Master_Bar_Summary <- Master_Violin %>%
  group_by(Group, Task, Context) %>%
  summarize(Average = mean(Ratio, na.rm = TRUE), 
            SD = sd(Ratio, na.rm = TRUE), 
            .groups = "drop")

Master_Bar_Summary$Context <- factor(Master_Bar_Summary$Context, levels = c("Subject of ser", "Subject of gustar", "Object of de"))
```


```{r, generate-proficiency-data}
## Create EPT data for proficiency
EPT_Proficiency <- Master %>% 
  filter(Task == "Production", !is.na(Comp_Use)) %>%
  group_by(Part_ID, Group, DELE, Context, Task) %>%
  summarize(Total_Structure = sum(Comp_Use, na.rm = TRUE),
            Total_Responses = sum(!is.na(Comp_Use)),
            Ratio = Total_Structure/Total_Responses,
            .groups = "drop") %>% 
  mutate(Ratio = Ratio * 100)


## Create FCT data for proficiency
FCT_Proficiency <- Master %>% 
  filter(Task == "Preference", !is.na(Comp_Use)) %>%
  group_by(Part_ID, Group, DELE, Context, Task) %>%
  summarize(Total_Structure = sum(Comp_Use, na.rm = TRUE),
            Total_Responses = sum(!is.na(Comp_Use)),
            Ratio = Total_Structure/Total_Responses,
            .groups = "drop") %>% 
  mutate(Ratio = Ratio * 100)


## Merge dataframes
Proficiency <- rbind(EPT_Proficiency, FCT_Proficiency)
```


```{r, generate-proficiency-summary}
DELE_Summary <- Master %>%
  distinct(Part_ID, Group, DELE) %>%
  group_by(Group) %>%
  summarize(
    N    = n(),
    Mean = mean(DELE, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD   = sd(DELE, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min  = min(DELE, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max  = max(DELE, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(c(Mean, SD), ~ round(.x, 1)),
         Group = recode(Group, "HS" = "Heritage Speakers", "L2L" = "L2 Learners"))
```

# Introduction


--
- Inflectional morphology is a well-known "bottleneck" of heritage (e.g., Slabakova, 2020) and L2 (e.g., Jensen et al., 2020) acquisition


--
- In Spanish, most studies have focused on:


--
  + Subjunctive mood (e.g., Solano-Escobar, 2025; Thane, 2025)
  
--
  + Differential object marking (e.g., Montrul et al., 2026; Hur, 2026)

--
  + Gender in articles and/or clitics (e.g., Meléndez et al., 2025; Shin et al., 2019)

--
  + Aspectual distinctions in the past tense (e.g., Cuza et al., 2013; Thane, 2023a)
  
--
  + Subject-verb agreement morphology (e.g., Alarcón, 2021; Foote, 2011)


--
- These areas often present learnability challenges:


--
  + Inflectional irregularities or nontransparent/noncanonical cues

--
  + Generally, some degree of involvement of the lexicon, semantics, or pragmatics (see Sorace, 2011)


---
# The case for nominalized infinitives


--
- **Nominalized Infinitives** (NIs) occur invariably (no co-occurrence of the gerund) in place of nouns, unlike English, as:


--
  + Subjects

--
  + Verbal direct objects

--
  + Prepositional objects


--
- Rather than telling a story of "simplification" (e.g., Silva-Corvalán, 2014), why not tell a story of robustness and resilience?


--
- Morphological infinitives are regular across the paradigm (easy to learn and master): <span class="verb-root">root</span> + <span class="verb-vowel">thematic vowel</span> + <span class="verb-r">r</span>

--

.verb-row[
.verb-col[
<div class="verb-display"><span class="verb-root">habl</span><span class="verb-vowel">a</span><span class="verb-r">r</span></div>
]

.verb-col[
<div class="verb-display"><span class="verb-root">sab</span><span class="verb-vowel">e</span><span class="verb-r">r</span></div>
]
]


--
- In sum, lower learnability challenges in bilinguals:


--
  + Perfect paradigmatic regularity

--
  + NIs are a case of core syntax (semantically-determined alternatives do not occur)


---
# Differences from English


--
- English nominalizes verbal forms quite distinctly, with lexically-selected options:

--
  + Only nominalized gerund

--
  + Only NI

--
  + Both nominalized gerund and NI
  

--
- 3 contexts studied in the present study:

--
  + Flexible verbs: gerunds *or* to-infinitives are acceptable in English

--
  + Gerund-only verbs: NIs in Spanish, nominalized gerunds only in English

--
  + Gerund-only prepositional objects: NIs in Spanish, nominalized gerunds only in English


--
- Patterns of language exposure and proficiency could affect the extent of crosslinguistic influence (Putnam & Sánchez, 2013; Sánchez, 2019)


--
  + Possible bilingual alignment for English-dominant bilinguals (transfer of gerunds)

--
  + Most likely for gerund-only verbs and gerund-only prepositional objects (divergence)


---
# Levels of (structured) variation

--
- Patterns of language use affect **individual** variation (Putnam & Sánchez, 2013)


--
- Heritage bilinguals (and L2 learners) show more stable access to syntax at the receptive level than in production (**within-speaker** variation; Perez-Cortes et al., 2019)


--
- Lexical frequency of individual items can affect production and preferences (**within-speaker** variation; e.g., Giancaspro, 2020; Hur, 2020; Sánchez, 2019; Thane, 2023a)


--
- When we take **individual** and **within-speaker variation** across syntactic contexts into account, we can observe **structured variation** (e.g., Shin, 2022; Shin et al., 2022)


--
- Two possibilities:

--
  + The high inflectional regularity and syntactic invariability of NIs makes them stable and resistant to crosslinguistic influence, showing stability

--
  + Individual-level and within-spekaer differences can predict variation, and it is structured within certain contexts


---
# A note on structured variation


--
- Structured variation is traditionally thought to be probabilistic and involve pattern generalizations (e.g., Shin, 2022)


--
- Recent studies have applied this approach to traditionally generative paradigms (e.g., Montrul et al., 2026; Shin et al., 2022)


--
- Variation can happen in monolingual and bilingual populations:

--
  + 16 Spanish-dominant bilingual adults, raised monolingually, did not show variation in use of NIs in this experiment


--
  + Exploring bilingual variation provides a more precise account of the complexities (*not the simplicities*) of heritage and L2 grammars


---
# Past research on NIs


--
- Some past research, albeit less than other inflectional areas


--
- Existing research with heritage speakers:


--
  + Escobar & Potowski (2015): some acceptance of gerunds; NIs accepted most with *ser* and prepositional objects


--
  + Belpoliti & Bermejo (2019): In writing samples, NIs are used 85% of the time, and gerunds 15%


--
  + Solano-Escobar & Cuza (2023): high production of/preference for NIs, but more gerunds in subject position


--
  + Cuza et al. (2025): proficiency and dominance affect children's overextension of gerunds, and more gerunds in oral production as prepositional objects


--
- Limited previous work with L2 learners


--
- Tendencies:

--
  + Some contexts seem to elicit more gerunds than others, but they differ across studies (structured)

--
  + Individual differences matter
  
--
  + Productive-receptive asymmetries and lexical-specific effects unclear


---
# Framework summary

--
- NIs are an area of possible strength and resilience, not one that is as likely to show deviation:

--
  + Core syntactic structure with a predictable paradigm

--
  + However, English crosslinguistic influence is possible (more complex, lexically-determined system)


--
- There may be structured variation and intraspeaker variation in the acquisition of NIs:

--
  + Different syntactic contexts (e.g., subject position, object of preposition)

--
  + Lexical frequency and task asymmetries could drive within-speaker differences


--
- Past research has not shown clear effects of one particular context over the other in heritage speakers


--
- Comparably little is known about L2 learners' NI systems, yet these speakers may have more persistent crosslinguistic influence from English given their later acquisition of Spanish

---
# Research questions


--
1. Do heritage speakers and L2 learners of Spanish show high rates of production of and preference for NIs?


--
2. Does syntactic context influence the production of/preference for NIs (main clause subject of *gustar*, subordinate clause subject of *ser*, prepositional object of *de*)?


--
3. Can proficiency level capture individual variation in NI production and preference?


--
4. Do heritage speakers and L2 learners show within-speaker variation on the basis of:


--
  + Production-preference asymmetries

--
  + Lexical frequency of the nominalized verb?


---
# Participants


--
- 34 adult heritage speakers (HS), mostly recruited from a large public research university

--
  + Wide dialectal diversity, not known yet to affect NI use

--
  + Did not receive dual language education, according to their reports


--
- 26 L2 learners (L2L), also attending the same university


--
- Participants were recruited from content courses, heritage courses, upper-level language bridge courses for L2Ls


--
```{r, proficiency-table}
Prof_Table <- DELE_Summary %>%
  kbl(caption = "<strong>DELE Proficiency Scores by Group</strong>",
      col.names = c("Group", "N", "Mean", "SD", "Min", "Max"),
      align = "c",
      escape = FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"))

Prof_Table
```


---
# Methods


--
- Data collected asynchronously online through Qualtrics and Phonic.ai


--
- 50-item lexical and morphosyntactic DELE exam, multiple choice


--
- Elicited **production** task (written prompt, oral response)


--
- Contextualized **preference** task (written prompt, select one of two written responses was best, either NI or gerund)


--
- Consistent syntactic contexts across production and preference:

--
  + 7 items as the subject of *ser* in a subordinate clause (*dice que _____ es muy divertido*), gerund preferred in English
  
--
  + 7 items as the subject of *gustar* as dative experiencer (*le gusta _____*), both infinitives and gerunds possible in English
  
--
  + 6 items as the object of the preposition *de* (*tiene miedo de _____*), only gerund accepted in English


--
- Methodological notes:

--
  + 1 item discarded from prepositions because it inadvertently did not follow the sentence frame
  
--
  + Same verbs on the production and preference tasks

--
  + Confound between *ser* in subordinate clause and *gustar* in main clause


---
# Variables of interest


--
- Group (HS as reference level, L2L; **group-level**)


--
- DELE score (standardized continuous predictor of proficiency; **individual-level**)


--
- Task (production as reference level, preference; **within-speaker**)


--
- Context (*ser* subject as reference level, *gustar* subject, *de* prepositional object; **within-speaker**)


--
- Lexical frequency (standardized value from Davies, 2016 corpus, found to be acceptable for heritage speakers in Thane, 2023; **within-speaker**)


--
- Group by task interaction


---
# Group-level summary

```{r, generate-summary-graphs}
# Bar graph
Bar_Graph <- Master_Bar_Summary %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = Context, y = Average, fill = Task)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge", color = "black", stat = "identity") +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(Group)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq (0, 105, 20),
                     limits = c(0, 105)) +
geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(Average), "\n(", round(SD), ")")),
          position = position_dodge(width = .9),
          vjust = 0.5,
          size = 6,
          fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#BF5700", "#F4EFE0")) +
  labs(x = "Average (SD) by context",
       y = "Percentage responses with infinitives",
       title = "") +
theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 20, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "none",
      strip.text = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
      strip.text.x = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"))


# Violin plot
Violin <- Master_Violin %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = Context, y = Ratio, fill = Task)) +
  geom_violin() +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(Group)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq (0, 105, 20),
                     limits = c(0, 105)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#BF5700", "#F4EFE0")) +
  labs(x = "Distribution by context", y = "Percentage of DOM responses",
       title = "") +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 20, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 16),
      strip.text = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
      strip.text.x = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
      axis.title.y = element_blank())


# Joint plot
Summary_Plot <- (Bar_Graph + Violin) + 
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Summary of Responses by Group, Context, and Task",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 28, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)))


# Print plot
(Summary_Plot)
```

# Overall correlations

```{r, generate-omnibus correlation}
# Generate correlation
Combined_Correlation <- glmer(Comp_Use ~ Group + DELE_Std + Task + Context + Davies_Std + Group:Task +
                    (1 + Context | Part_ID) + (1 | Item),
                  data = Master,
                  family = binomial,
                  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa",
                                         optCtrl = list(maxfun = 10000)))


# Generate forest plot
Combined_Correlation_Plot <- plot_model(Combined_Correlation, show.values = TRUE, show.intercept = TRUE, value.offset = .3, transform = NULL, vline.color = "black") +
          scale_x_discrete(labels = c("L2L * Preference", "Lexical frequency", "Object of de", "Subject of gustar", "Preference task", "Proficiency", "L2 Learners", "(Intercept)")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-15, 15, 3),
                       limits = c(-15, 15)) +
  labs(title = "Overall model", y = "Estimates") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 24, face = "bold"))


# Print forest plot
(Combined_Correlation_Plot)
```

# Production correlation

```{r, generate-production-correlation}
Production_Correlation <- glmer(Comp_Use ~ Group + DELE_Std + Context + Davies_Std +
                                (1 + Context | Part_ID) + (1 | Item),
                              data = Master %>% filter(Task == "Production"),
                              family = binomial,
                              control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa",
                                                     optCtrl = list(maxfun = 10000)))


# Generate forest plot
Production_Correlation_Plot <- plot_model(Production_Correlation, show.values = TRUE, show.intercept = TRUE, value.offset = .3, transform = NULL, vline.color = "black") +
      scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Lexical frequency", "Object of de", "Subject of gustar", "Proficiency", "L2 Learners", "(Intercept)")) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-15, 15, 3),
                       limits = c(-15, 15)) +
  labs(title = "Production model", y = "Estimates") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 24, face = "bold"))


# Print forest plot
(Production_Correlation_Plot)
```

---
# Summary of results


--
- No group-level differences in overall data between L2 learners and heritage speakers


--
- No significant task effect (nor descriptive evidence of such)

--
  + L2 learners show more consistent NI preference (significant)

--
  + Group and task alone cannot account for findings

--
- No effect of lexical frequency


--
- Clear effect for context:

--
  + Subject of ser (subordinate, but straightforward, optional NI in English) was significantly more challenging

--
  + Prepositional object of *de* also less frequently elicited NIs than *gustar* subjects


---
# Discussion: Research questions


--
- No group-level differences detected (RQ1); L2Ls showed more asymmetrical performance between production and selection


--
- Individual-level proficiency effects found (RQ2), especially in the more variable context as the subject of *ser* in subordinate clauses among HSs


--
- Structured variation found where the gerund is preferred in English as the subject of *ser*, but not where it is required, as in the case of the object of the preposition *de*


--
  + Could challenges be due to the increased processing cost of subordinate clauses?

--
  + Consistent results for gerunds in subject position with Solano-Escobar & Cuza (2023)
  
--
  + Consistent use of infinitives in prepositional object position in Escobar & Potowski (2015)

--
  + Dissonant results from Escobar & Potowski (2015) regarding *ser*


--
- No within-speaker variation as a function of task asymmetry or lexical frequency (RQ4), but L2Ls showed more asymmetry between tasks than HSs


--
- Conjecture: Infinitives are less prone to within-speaker variation because they have fewer learnability challenges:

--
  + This does not mean structured variation does not occur

--
  + Simpler morphological paradigms and core syntactic learning result in resilience, even in the face of crosslinguistic influence (most of the time)


---
